title: odd-even-token-batching-runbook
body:
Background:

This is a messy personal notebook for an exploratory idea: instead of using purely size-based packing for request batching, attempt a fast, deterministic parity bucketing on token counts (odd vs even). Hypothesis: predictable parity buckets reduce packing fragmentation for small variable-length requests and produce more consistent batch formation latency while being cheap to compute in the front proxy.

Why parity?
- Minimal computation on the ingress path (token_count % 2).
- For many apps we observed a bimodal token-length distribution around short prompts (1-6 tokens) and medium prompts (20-60 tokens). Parity tends to split many small requests into balanced substreams, often avoiding a single long request delaying a mixed batch.
- Easy to route to two microqueues per backend worker. Low ops overhead.

Experiment goals:
1) Measure end-to-end p50/p95/p99 generation latency impact under mixed traffic.
2) Track GPU utilization and kernel launch overhead changes.
3) Observe cold-cache warmup behavior and whether parity buckets help reduce cold-path variance.
4) Quantify cost/tradeoffs: increased queueing complexity vs latency tail reductions.

Setup:
- Target model: open-llama-13b-8k-quant (quantized runtime image).
- Fleet: 8xA100 (hosts configured identical), each host runs 4 worker processes -> 32 workers.
- Ingress proxy: local mock that can do parity bucketing or baseline round-robin.
- Load driver: custom wrk-like driver that replays production trace slices (trace id: trace-2024-05-multi) with synthetic amplification to target QPS.
- Sequence lengths: sample distribution derived from prod slice: short(45%), medium(40%), long(15%).
- Workload profiles: steady (10k qps total), bursty (10s ramps to 30k qps), and mixed-background (steady 6k + sporadic 25k microburst every 120s).
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (generation start -> last token), server-side batch sizes, GPU SM util, per-worker batch formation time, KV cache hit ratio, and token throughput.

Runs summary (abridged):
- Baseline (no parity): steady @10k qps: p50 82ms, p95 210ms, p99 480ms; avg batch size 3.2, GPU util 58%.
- Parity buckets enabled (2 lanes): steady @10k qps: p50 78ms, p95 185ms, p99 390ms; avg batch size per-lane 2.9/3.1, aggregate similar but fewer mixed long+short batches. GPU util 56% (slightly lower).
- Bursty profile (ramp to 30k): baseline p99 spikes to 1.2s during ramp crest; parity p99 spikes to 760ms. Notable: parity reduced worst-case queueing delay by ~40% during rapid inflows.
- Mixed-background: parity reduced cold-path p95 by ~22% and reduced variance of first-token latencies when cache was cold.

Observations and notes:
- Batch purity: Parity produced batches with higher homogeneity (more similar token lengths inside batch), which reduced decoding time variance. This matters because for kernel selection we pick path based on expected seq length; homogeneous batches avoid fallback to slow generic kernels.
- Slight throughput loss: GPU util down ~2% on steady runs. Likely due to narrower batching windows per lane causing more small batches hitting the hardware. But net per-token latency and tail improved. Cost/unit increased marginally; need to quantify in cost/unit test.
- Warmup behaviour: when enabling parity, one lane would sometimes be underfilled for long stretches if client traffic skewed to a particular parity for several minutes. This lead to transient lower throughput on that lane and an imbalance in GPU scheduling. We added a cheap "lane-drain" policy in the proxy: if lane idle > 15s and opposite lane has > 2 queued requests, allow cross-merge up to N so GPUs don't starve. That restored throughput balance with small tail cost.
- Edge case: A long streaming request with 300 tokens blocked an otherwise-even lane; parity didn't help if the long request was dominant. Need fallback: detect long-header and route to dedicated long-lane.
- Kernel warm-start overhead was slightly lower because batches had fewer sequence-length outliers; GPU kernels could amortize setup across similar-length sequences.

Telemetry excerpts (not raw CSV, just highlights):
- Run 17 (burst): baseline p99 1.21s -> parity p99 0.78s (35% reduction).
- Run 24 (steady, peak minute sample): baseline avg token/sec 148k -> parity 144k (2.7% drop).
- KV cache hit ratio: baseline 62% -> parity 61% (no material change).
- Median batch formation time (worker-side): baseline 6.4ms -> parity 5.1ms (weird but reproducible; possibly because per-lane queues saw more consistent arrival spacing).

Quick conclusions:
- Parity bucketing is a cheap, low-compute heuristic that materially reduces tail latency under mixed/bursty workloads at the cost of a small drop in throughput efficiency.
- The improvement is pronounced during rapid ingress ramps where mixed-size packing causes long request blocking.
- Implementing lightweight fallback/merge rules is necessary to avoid long-term lane imbalance.
- Not a silver bullet for workloads dominated by single long requests or strongly skewed parity distributions.

Recommended next steps:
1) Run a longer economics sweep: 48h A/B comparing cost-per-1M tokens served at production mixes to determine if tail savings offset throughput loss.
2) Implement a third "long-lane" for requests > X tokens and measure overall efficiency. Could be dynamically sized (probe small fraction of traffic to calibrate X).
3) Add fast-probe instrumentation in the front proxy to compute per-client parity skew and adapt lane thresholds per-client (if a client always sends even-length prompts, we should avoid penalizing them).
4) Confirm with other models: run on a smaller LLaMA-7B and a large decoder-heavy LLM to validate kernel impacts.
5) Draft a short design note for eng-serving-runtime and a test PR for the gateway with an opt-in flag and telemetry hooks.

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self):
- Need to formalize merge thresholds and safety limits for lane-drain (current values are heuristic).
- How does parity interact with multi-tenant scheduling where a worker hosts multiple tenants? Could parity create tenant-level starvation?
- Investigate whether N>2 lanes (mod 3 or mod 5 bucketing) yields better throughput/tail tradeoffs; cost of extra lanes increases control complexity.
- Is there a simple way to use request arrival timestamp jitter to decide when to merge lanes vs wait?

Run artifacts and commands used (cheat-sheet):
- Driver: bin/trace_replay --trace trace-2024-05-multi --amplify 3 --pattern mixed
- Proxy test branch: git@github.com:redwood-inference/gateway.git#odd-even-buckets
- Analysis scripts: bench/odd_even_agg.py (produces aggregated latency percentiles + per-lane batch histograms)
- Quick local check: scripts/sim_parity_queue.py --qps 10000 --dist sample.json

Notes to collaborators: Ravi/Ivy please eyeball the lane-drain parameters I left at 15s/2/3 and tell me if those thresholds make sense from a deployment-safety POV. Also would appreciate a quick run on a 4xA10 testbed if you have spare capacity — I'm concerned about the small throughput drop amplifying on smaller GPUs.

End of messy notebook. Will convert the promising parts into a PR and a more formal evaluation notebook if the team wants to pursue.

— Camila
